title: Grade 6 Computer Science: Computers & Coding Basics

learn: A computer is a machine that takes input, processes it, stores it and produces output.
Input devices include keyboards, mice, microphones and touchscreens. Output devices include screens, speakers and printers.
Computers follow instructions called programs.
lessons.try: List five input and five output devices in your home.

learn: Hardware is the physical parts you can touch: the processor (CPU), memory and storage.
Software is the programs that run on hardware: apps, games and operating systems.
The operating system (like Windows, macOS or Android) manages the computer.
lessons.try: Sort a list into hardware and software.

learn: RAM is short-term memory that holds what the computer is working on right now; it empties when power is off.
Storage (hard drives, SSDs) keeps files even when power is off.
Storage is measured in bytes: kilobytes, megabytes, gigabytes, terabytes.
check: A gigabyte is bigger than a...
lessons.try: Find how much storage a device you use has.

learn: Computers store everything as bits: 0s and 1s.
Binary is a base-2 number system. Each place is worth double the one to its right: 1, 2, 4, 8, 16...
lessons.try: Write the numbers 1 to 10 in binary.

learn: Eight bits make one byte, which can store 256 different values.
Each letter is stored as a number. In ASCII, "A" is 65.
Unicode allows letters from every language and even emoji.
lessons.try: Write your initials as ASCII numbers.

learn: Digital images are made of pixels, each stored as numbers for red, green and blue.
Sound is stored by measuring the sound wave thousands of times a second.
More pixels or more samples mean better quality but bigger files.
check: Colours are stored as amounts of...
lessons.try: Zoom into a digital photo until you see pixels.

learn: An algorithm is a precise, step-by-step set of instructions to solve a problem.
Recipes and directions are everyday algorithms.
Algorithms must be clear and in the right order.
lessons.try: Write an algorithm for making a sandwich, then have someone follow it exactly.

learn: Sequencing means putting steps in the correct order.
Computers do exactly what they are told, in order.
A wrong order gives wrong results: putting on shoes before socks.
lessons.try: Put scrambled steps of brushing teeth in the right order.

learn: Flowcharts show algorithms with shapes: ovals for start/end, rectangles for steps, diamonds for decisions.
Pseudocode writes algorithms in plain language that looks like code.
Both help plan before coding.
check: Decisions in a flowchart use a...
Plain language that looks like code
lessons.try: Draw a flowchart for deciding what to wear based on the weather.

learn: A loop repeats instructions so you don't have to write them again.
"Repeat 4 times: move forward, turn right" draws a square.
Loops make programs shorter and easier to change.
check: Repeat 4 times: move, turn right draws a...
lessons.try: Write a loop to draw a triangle.

learn: A count loop (for loop) repeats a set number of times.
A condition loop (while loop) repeats while something is true: "while not at the wall, move forward".
Be careful: a loop that never stops is an infinite loop.
check: A loop that never stops is...
lessons.try: Write a while loop to fill a glass until it's full.

learn: A nested loop is a loop inside another loop.
"Repeat 3 times: (repeat 4 times: draw a side, turn)" draws three squares.
Nested loops are used for grids, like rows and columns of a game board.
check: A loop inside a loop is a...
lessons.try: Plan a nested loop that draws a 3-by-3 grid of dots.

learn: A conditional makes a decision: "if it is raining, take an umbrella".
The condition is a question with a true or false answer.
Code inside the if runs only when the condition is true.
check: If code runs when the condition is...
lessons.try: Write three if statements about your daily life.

learn: If-else gives two paths: "if score > 10, say 'You win', else say 'Try again'".
Else-if adds more choices.
Only one path runs.
check: How many paths run in an if-else?
lessons.try: Write an if-else for a game that checks if a guess is right.

learn: Comparison operators: = (equal), < (less than), > (greater than).
AND means both must be true; OR means at least one is true; NOT flips true and false.
"If age > 12 AND has ticket" checks two conditions.
lessons.try: Write a condition for "you can play if you've finished homework OR it's the weekend".

learn: A variable is a named container that stores a value, like score = 0.
The value can change as the program runs: score = score + 1.
Good names describe what is stored: "lives", not "x".
check: Which is a good variable name?
lessons.try: List variables a racing game might use.

learn: Numbers (integers and decimals), text (strings) and true/false (Booleans) are common data types.
"Hello" is a string; 42 is an integer; true is a Boolean.
Lists store many values: ["apple", "banana", "cherry"].
lessons.try: Sort ten example values into data types.

learn: Programs read input into variables: name = ask("What's your name?").
Variables can be combined: "Hello " + name.
Counters and timers in games are variables.
lessons.try: Plan a program that counts how many times you click a button.

learn: An event is something that happens that a program responds to: a click, a key press or a timer.
"When the space key is pressed, jump" is an event handler.
Games and apps are built on events.
check: Code that responds to an event is an...
lessons.try: List five events in a game you play.

learn: Sprites are characters or objects in a program.
Sprites can move, change costume, play sounds and respond to events.
Collisions (touching) are common events in games.
lessons.try: Design a simple game where a sprite collects stars.

learn: Plan a game with a goal, rules, controls and a way to win or lose.
Use variables for score and lives, loops for movement, conditionals for rules.
Test with players and improve it.
lessons.try: Write a one-page design for your own game.

learn: A bug is an error in a program that makes it behave wrongly.
Syntax errors break the rules of the language; logic errors give wrong results.
Grace Hopper's team found a real moth in a computer in 1947 and taped it in their logbook as the "first actual case of bug being found".
check: An error in a program is a...
The famous moth was found in...
lessons.try: Find the bug in a short set of written instructions.

learn: Read the error message carefully.
Test small parts one at a time.
Explain your code out loud (rubber-duck debugging) to spot mistakes.
check: Test ___ parts one at a time.
The first thing to check is the...
lessons.try: Explain a program to a toy, line by line.

learn: Testing checks that a program works as planned.
Try normal inputs, edge cases (like 0 or very large numbers) and wrong inputs.
Keep a list of tests and results.
lessons.try: Write five tests for a calculator program.

learn: Decomposition breaks a big problem into smaller, manageable parts.
Making a game: design characters, build levels, write rules, add sound.
Smaller parts are easier to solve and test.
lessons.try: Decompose planning a birthday party into steps.

learn: A function is a named block of code that does one job: drawSquare().
Call the function whenever you need it instead of rewriting code.
Functions keep programs organised.
lessons.try: Write a function to draw a star, then use it three times.

learn: Parameters let functions work with different values: drawSquare(size).
Abstraction hides details so you can focus on what matters.
You use a microwave without knowing how it works inside: that's abstraction.
lessons.try: Change a drawSquare function to take a size parameter.

learn: Digital citizens use technology safely, respectfully and responsibly.
Think before you post: posts can be permanent and shared widely.
Treat people online the way you'd treat them in person.
lessons.try: Make a poster with five rules for good digital citizenship.

learn: Strong passwords are long and mix letters, numbers and symbols.
Never share personal information with strangers.
Phishing messages try to trick you into giving away information.
lessons.try: Create a strong password pattern you could remember (don't share it).

learn: Computers changed communication, medicine, transport and entertainment.
Ada Lovelace wrote what is considered the first computer program in 1843.
New technology brings benefits and challenges, like screen time and fairness.
check: Who wrote the first computer program?
Ada Lovelace's program was written in...
lessons.try: Discuss one benefit and one challenge of a technology you use.
